summary:
On Earth, if you get lost, you open your phone and search your exact location on Google Maps or other app. On Mars there are no roads, no GPS, no taxis. ARES-TWIN is a decision-support copilot and training simulator that lets an astronaut rehearse a Martian walk before it counts for real. Existing Mars maps show what is there; but ARES-TWIN answers the question an astronaut actually asks: “Can I explore and still make it back?”

We combined real NASA data from Gale Crater and Mount Sharp (USGS DEM, HiRISE imagery, CRISM mineral spectra, and MGS TES thermal context) into a terrain cost map. Using oxygen as the single currency, an experimental Pandolf-Santee-based model adapted to Mars gravity (~0.38 g) estimates the metabolic effort of every leg, so it knows that climbing costs more than descending. A* finds low-cost routes, CTOPTW selects which science sites to visit and in what order, and a reverse Dijkstra check keeps a configurable reserve for the return. If a hazard appears, a site falls into shadow, the astronaut tires, or a solar storm hits, the route is replanned in under 2 seconds.

Three synchronized views (astronaut first person, third person, and a conceptual reconnaissance drone) show the same mission. Beyond Mars, ARES-TWIN could support lunar missions, rescue teams in the Amazon, and astronaut training. Explore smarter. Navigate safer. Discover Mars.
details:
ARES-TWIN is a decision-support copilot and training simulator for a human Marswalk. Existing Mars tools such as Mars Trek and the geologic mapping layers show what is on the surface, but they are built for regional and global views. An astronaut on a spacewalk needs a different answer: “Can I reach my science targets and still make it back safely?”

We chose Mount Sharp in Gale Crater, where Curiosity studied boxwork formations, so our science objective is to guide an astronaut to sites of geological interest. The system integrates four layers of real NASA data:

  • Topographic: USGS Mars MSL Gale Merged DEM (~1 m), used to derive slope, elevation change and roughness.
  • Optical: MRO HiRISE (~0.25 m/pixel), used to identify rocks, textures and possible obstacles.
  • Spectral: MRO CRISM (~18 m/pixel), used to flag mineral signatures such as hematite and clays, which become science priorities.
  • Thermal: MGS TES nighttime thermal inertia (~3 km), used only as coarse regional context, not as a local or metre-scale measurement.

These layers are aligned and combined into a terrain cost map. Each cell stores not just distance but the effort of crossing it, so the shortest path is not necessarily the best one.

How it works

  1. Oxygen as the single currency. An experimental model based on Pandolf-Santee, adapted to Mars gravity (~0.38 g), estimates the metabolic effort of each leg from slope, terrain, walking speed and carried mass. The result is converted into an equivalent oxygen demand. This is a metabolic estimate, not the real consumption of a spacesuit, and the model has not been validated on Mars.
  2. Route planning. A* finds the lowest-cost path across the cost map. CTOPTW (branch-and-bound, 2 s time limit) chooses which science sites to visit and in what order. A reverse Dijkstra evaluates the return from every site, so the plan always keeps a configurable reserve (15% or 25%) to get back.
  3. Safety first. Hard constraints block unsafe terrain, and a science reward can never outweigh a safety condition. An alert mechanism and a mission-abort threshold are part of the rules.
  4. Real-time replanning. If a hazard appears, a site falls into shadow, the astronaut tires or a solar storm alert arrives, the route is replanned in under 2 seconds.

Three synchronized views of one mission

  • Astronaut first person (POV): the main experience. The route, direction, slope warnings, science points and risk zones are overlaid on the terrain, with critical information kept clear and uncluttered.
  • Astronaut third person: a full-body astronaut on the terrain, showing traveled path, remaining route, progress and human scale.
  • Reconnaissance drone: an aerial view that scouts sectors the astronaut has not yet reached, showing the cost map, unverified areas and alternative routes. The drone is a future concept used to reduce uncertainty ahead of the astronaut, not an existing Mars aircraft.

    All three views share the same mission state, so a move, alert or replan appears consistently in each.

Virtual reality (VR)

ARES-TWIN includes a functional VR mode that places the user inside the astronaut’s helmet. The headset view reproduces the astronaut’s first-person perspective, so the visor of the VR device acts as the visor of the spacesuit: the user looks around the Martian terrain at human height and sees the recommended route, direction markers, slope warnings, science targets and risk zones overlaid on the landscape, exactly as the astronaut would see them.

VR conveys what a flat map cannot: the true scale of slopes, rocks and distances, and how much effort a route demands. Because the VR view shares the same mission state as the other two perspectives, every movement, alert or route replan is reflected consistently across all of them. This makes VR both an operational interface and a training tool: students and future astronauts can walk the planned route and practice go/abort decisions before a real mission, in a safe environment where mistakes cost nothing.

Astronaut vital signs and state

The system links the human body to route planning. A vitals panel tracks the astronaut’s physiological state (for example: heart rate, metabolic load, estimated oxygen use, fatigue level]) and compares it with configurable thresholds. When the astronaut tires or a threshold is crossed, the system raises an alert and recommends a new plan, such as a shorter route or an earlier return. In the prototype, these values are simulated telemetry, not real medical data, and the system is not a validated medical device.

Tools and technologies

The project is mostly Python (95.7%), complemented by TypeScript (1.5%), C (0.9%), HTML (0.8%), Cython (0.7%) and C++ (0.2%). Python handles geospatial processing, the terrain cost map, the metabolic effort model and the planning algorithms (A*, CTOPTW and reverse Dijkstra). Cython, C and C++ accelerate the computationally heavy parts so that replanning stays fast.

The backend is served with FastAPI, which exposes the mission state, routes, alerts and events to the interface through structured JSON messages. This lets every module and every view read from the same source of truth. Scientific data are handled as GeoTIFF/COG rasters for the NASA layers (DEM, HiRISE, CRISM and TES), CSV/Parquet for tabular records, glTF for 3D models such as the astronaut, and JSON for events, states and contracts. Each variable keeps its source, resolution, unit and processing history, so real NASA data, derived variables, assumptions and simulated data are never mixed up. TypeScript and HTML power the interface and the visualization of the three synchronized views: astronaut first person, astronaut third person and the conceptual reconnaissance drone.

What makes it creative and different

  • Oxygen as the single currency: every decision is expressed in the resource that actually limits an astronaut, instead of kilometers or minutes.
  • It plans the return, not just the arrival: the reverse Dijkstra check means no route is recommended unless the astronaut can get back.
  • Science plus safety in one model: CRISM mineral interest rewards the route, but safety constraints always win.
  • Human-centered: the body, the carried mass and the 0.38 g gravity shape the map, so the same terrain costs a different amount going up than going down.
  • Three perspectives, one mission: first person, third person and the aerial scout together answer “what do I see, where am I, and what is ahead?”
  • VR training: the same planner doubles as a rehearsal tool, where decisions can be practiced before they count.
  • Honest by design: every layer carries its resolution and source, and we clearly separate real NASA data, derived variables, assumptions, simulated data and conceptual features.

Benefits and intended impact

With communication delays to Earth, the go/abort decision falls on the astronaut. ARES-TWIN gives them an explainable, data-based recommendation so they can explore more science without risking the return. Beyond Mars, the same approach applies to the Moon and Artemis surface missions, to rescue teams searching for someone in difficult terrain such as the Amazon rainforest, and to education, where students and future astronauts can train their decisions in a safe virtual environment.

Limitations and future work

The effort model is experimental, TES is a coarse regional layer, the sinkage value is only a proxy, and the drone and any live telemetry are conceptual or simulated. Future work includes validating the model, adding higher-resolution thermal data such as THEMIS, and integrating real space weather and radiation data.
